divisions.question: Lisa Chesters What an extraordinary question time—again the government denied the link between pay and safety when it comes to roads and what has been decided by the tribunal. Let me remind the government what the Australian Productivity Commission report found in 2016. This is a government that is happy to support the Productivity Commission when they recommend cutting penalty rates but is not willing to support the Productivity Commission when they say there is a direct link between pay and safety. The cherry-picking of this government is extraordinary. And that is not the only report that linked pay to safety on our roads. There was another report, by Jaguar Consulting, in 2014. There was the National Transport Commission report in 2008. The Productivity Commission recognised in 2014 and 2016 that RSOS will result in a '10 per cent to 18 per cent reduction in the number of crashes'. This is on page 86, if government members would like to check it out. Perhaps they should read up on it before they make a statement in this House stating otherwise. The road transport industry has the highest fatality rate of any industry in Australia, with fatality rates 12 times higher than the average for other industries. That was on page 6 of the Productivity Commission review. Let me just state that again: '12 times higher'. Let's be real about our roads network. It is the workplace of Australian truck drivers. It is the responsibility of this place to do everything it can to ensure that safety is paramount on our roads, yet all the government plans to do—what they believe will improve road safety—is just build roads. That is not enough. It is not enough to just build roads. You also have to look at who is driving on our roads and the pressure on our truck drivers on our roads. In my previous statement I listed example after example of trucking accidents in my electorate. The Bendigo electorate has a vast network of highways. Michaelia Cash I move: That this bill be now read a second time. I seek leave to have the second reading speech incorporated in _Hansard_. Leave granted. _The speech read as follows—_ The Government is introducing the _Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill_because this Government stands by owner drivers and mum and dad small businesses who just want to earn an honest living. It has been clear for some time that the Road Safety Remuneration System, established in 2012 by the former Labor Government, has demonstrated no tangible safety outcomes for the road transport industry. Two separate, comprehensive, evidence based reviews have supported this in the strongest of terms. Even Labor's own regulatory analysis completed at the time the System was introduced acknowledged that there was insufficient evidence to demonstrate a clear link between road safety and remuneration. There is nothing fair or safe about the Road Safety Remuneration System and that is why the Coalition Government has listened to thousands of owner drivers across the country and put this very urgent bill before the House today. The refusal of the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal to listen to reason and delay the commencement of the 2016 Payments Order in the face of widespread confusion and misunderstanding is the last straw. Around 800 submissions were made to the Tribunal. Almost all of these called for a delay to the Payments Order, with many indicating that the Order will negatively impact their business and, in a number of cases, put them out of business altogether. Even in the face of this evidence, the Tribunal refused to delay the start date of the Payments Order to allow these small businesses time to try to comply. I note that, notwithstanding the Transport Workers Union's strong opposition to any delay, the TWU is before the Tribunal today, seeking to delay the payments in the Order to 1 January 2017. speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: The House was asked to suspend standing orders to allow the immediate introduction and debate of the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 [No. 3], the Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill 2016, and the Road Safety Remuneration Amendment (Protecting Owner Drivers) Bill 2016. The speaker argued the Fair Work bill, passed three times by the House, targets dishonest union leaders, while the Road Safety bills address the impact on owner drivers from Labor’s previous legislation.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: The government introduced the Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill 2016, arguing the Road Safety Remuneration System has not improved safety and will cost the economy over $2 billion over 15 years, while redirecting $4 million annually to the National Heavy Vehicle Regulator.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: The government introduced the Road Safety Remuneration Amendment (Protecting Owner Drivers) Bill to suspend the contractor-driver minimum payments order until 1 January 2017, arguing it is causing financial hardship for 35,000 truck drivers and their families. The government's preferred option remains full abolition of the road safety remuneration system.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: The speaker argued against repealing the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal, citing 25 heavy-vehicle-related road deaths last month and over 300 last year, and presenting evidence from PwC, NTC, and academic reports that link pay rates to safety. He named truck driver John Waltis, who had attended 52 funerals of killed drivers, and quoted Senator John Williams and researchers Michael Quinlan and Michael Belzer in support of the tribunal's role in preventing unsafe practices.

speeches.speaker: Mark Coulton
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal should be repealed because it discriminates against owner-driver truck drivers by imposing above-market rates that only apply to them, not to large companies or employed drivers, causing owner-operators to lose contracts and park their trucks. The speaker cited examples of a driver named Greg from Melbourne and a contractor from Tomingley who could no longer compete, and noted that the coalition opposed the tribunal when it was established in 2012.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Bird
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill 2016, arguing the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal addresses structural issues in the trucking industry that lead to high death and suicide rates, and criticised opponents for demonising unions instead of tackling systemic problems.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: The speaker argued against the Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill, defending the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal as an independent umpire that improves road safety through measures like mandatory drug testing and safe driving plans, and cited a PwC report predicting a 10–18% reduction in crashes. The speaker criticised the Turnbull government for politicising the tribunal and accused the Prime Minister of changing his position for political gain.

speeches.speaker: Rick Wilson
speeches.brief: The member for O'Connor argued that the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal's findings would destroy owner-driver family businesses in his electorate, citing impacts on grain, livestock, and general freight haulage, and noted his own multi-combination driver's licence as relevant experience.

speeches.speaker: Scott Buchholz
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill 2016 should be passed to abolish the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal, claiming the tribunal's remuneration order would force owner-drivers out of business by imposing unworkable inflated rates, and that over 200 drivers protested in Canberra against the legislation.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: The Labor speaker opposed the Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill 2016, arguing that abolishing the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal would increase road deaths by removing minimum pay and safety standards for truck drivers. They cited a fatality rate 12 times the national average and studies showing a direct link between higher pay and safer driving, with a 40% decline in crash probability for every 10% increase in mileage pay rates.

speeches.speaker: Rowan Ramsey
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal is a Labor-union initiative that unfairly targets owner-operator truck drivers, and supported the repeal bill to prevent a ruling that would impose minimum rates and cost the economy $2.3 billion over 15 years while threatening 3,500 jobs. He named several owner-operators from South Australia who would be driven out of business, and criticised the shadow minister for linking the tribunal's ruling to a fatal accident without evidence.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Moved to suspend standing order 133 (deferred divisions on Mondays and Tuesdays) until the conclusion of consideration of the Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill 2016 and the Road Safety Remuneration Amendment (Protecting Owner Drivers) Bill 2016, to allow a vote on the RSRT at the earliest convenience of the House.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Hastie
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill, arguing that the 2016 payments order from the tribunal harms small trucking businesses and regional supermarkets, and cited owner-operator Glen Morris's costs and two reviews that found no link between remuneration and road safety.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill 2016, arguing that the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal should be retained because evidence—including reports from 2000, 2001, 2006, 2008, and 2010—establishes a link between pay and road safety, and that abolishing it was a politically motivated attack on workers that would increase road fatalities, noting 25 deaths from heavy vehicle accidents in the past month and a fatality rate 12 times the national average.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal order was designed to make owner-drivers uncompetitive and destroy small businesses, citing a $54,000 fine threat to contractor Bryan Alley, and announced the Road Safety Remuneration Amendment (Protecting Owner Drivers) Bill 2016 as a backup to defer the order until 2017 if the Senate rejects the repeal bill.

speeches.speaker: Ken O'Dowd
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the passage of the Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill 2016 was a success, receiving thanks from truckies like Heath Nowland of Gracemere and Julie Just, and that it allows 35,000 owner-drivers to return to work.
